messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 75, Kai, a widowed financial analyst of Oceania heritage, had spent the last twelve years navigating a life quietly reshaped by a single night of violation. Twelve years prior, while reviewing offshore ledgers in a late-night corporate office, a senior partner used his positional power to corner Kai in a locked conference room. The assault was absolute, stripping away any remaining trust in institutional safety. When Kai fled the building and contacted the responding police officer, the encounter compounded the trauma: the officer did not offer protection, but instead criticized Kai’s disjointed account, dismissing the moral violation and fixating on procedural discrepancies. That night, Kai attempted to reconstruct the event, but the narrative kept fracturing into disjointed flashes. There was no coherent story, only the sudden return of a coppery taste and the phantom echo of keys scraping against linoleum. Over the following months, these sensory intrusions began to dictate daily routines, and the clinical picture of profound distress took root. The cycle tightened quickly, anchored by how the mind and body responded to ordinary moments. Whenever a compliance auditor’s tone grew sharp or a senior colleague leaned over to correct a spreadsheet figure, the authority presence instantly fractured Kai’s focus, dragging the same disjointed, taste-laden memories back into the room. Those intrusive recollections did not merely flash; they actively dismantled Kai’s sense of mental stability. The auditory echoes of the assault, combined with the complete inability to tell a clear story of what occurred, convinced Kai that their cognitive processes were failing. The fear of going crazy grew from a whispered doubt into a daily conviction, rooted entirely in the very memories that refused to settle into a logical sequence. Because Kai could no longer trust their own recollection, they began to abandon the analytical routines that had once defined their career, convinced that their own judgment was fundamentally compromised. This erosion of self-trust extended into every professional and personal interaction. Each instance of correction or observed moral violation reinforced Kai’s conviction that they could no longer rely on themselves to navigate the world safely, deepening the sense that nothing in their work or home held any meaningful weight. The avoidance that once felt protective gradually became a rigid architecture: Kai stopped attending partner meetings, requested fully remote audits, and altered their commute to bypass precincts that triggered the authority presence. Yet the loop tightened without mercy. Because the vivid memories would surface during quiet hours, the coppery taste and echoing footsteps made any future encounter with authority or correction feel like an imminent threat, pulling the triggers tighter with every recurrence. When a junior analyst once questioned a variance report with pointed correction, the sensory flashback returned so forcefully that Kai had to leave the conference room, heart hammering, only to return later with trembling hands to manually verify every entry they could no longer trust themselves to calculate. The isolation persisted until last winter, when a routine physical exam flagged escalating anxiety, insomnia, and the toll of years spent performing professional duties while internally fracturing. Reluctantly, Kai scheduled an intake with a trauma specialist, hoping to find a way to quiet the intrusive tastes and sounds that had hijacked their daily existence. What Kai fears most now is that the memories will continue to warp their perception of authority and criticism until nothing of their former identity remains. More than anything, they are hoping to reclaim a stable narrative, one that does not taste of fear or echo with the sounds of violation, so they might finally trust themselves again.
